questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Outline the steps that turn a no-effect level into an intake limit.
questions.stem: Our revision notes on deriving a daily intake limit start at the animal study and end with a number for residents.

options.text: Take the lowest dose that caused harm in the study, since it is the most protective figure available to us.
options.misconception: uses a lowest effect level as the intake limit

options.text: Divide the no-effect level by uncertainty factors covering species, individuals, study length and database gaps.
Average the no-effect levels from every study we can find, so the limit reflects all the evidence.
options.misconception: averages study results instead of choosing a basis

options.text: Use the no-effect level directly, because it is the highest dose with no effects in the study.
options.misconception: treats a no-effect level as a safe limit

questions.explanation: A no-effect level is an observation from one study, so uncertainty factors cover the gaps between animals and people, between people, and between short studies and lifetime exposure.
questions.hint: Start from the no-effect level and discount it.

questions.learningObjective: Add absorbed doses arriving by inhalation and by ingestion.

options.text: The total absorbed dose is 50 mg, because both amounts are added before any absorption is considered.
options.misconception: adds ingested and inhaled amounts without absorption

options.text: The total absorbed dose is 39 mg, but it must be divided by body weight before it can be used.
options.misconception: omits the body weight step entirely

options.text: The total absorbed dose is 12 mg, because only the inhaled contribution reaches the blood unchanged.
options.misconception: ignores the oral route contribution

options.text: The total absorbed dose is 39 mg, since 20 times 0.6 is 12 mg and 30 times 0.9 is 27 mg.

questions.explanation: Each route contributes its own absorbed amount, and 12 mg from the lung plus 27 mg from the gut gives 39 mg absorbed. Divide that by body weight to obtain a dose per kilogram.
questions.hint: Absorb each route, then add them.

questions.stem: Revision notes: a fish from our survey held 0.15 mg per kg of body weight, while the water it swam in held 0.005 mg per litre.
questions.explanation: The bioconcentration factor is tissue concentration over water concentration, so 0.15 divided by 0.005 is 30 litres per kilogram. The ratio is only valid at steady state.

options.text: The biomagnification factor is predator concentration over prey concentration, and each step adds a fixed amount.
options.misconception: treats biomagnification as additive across steps

options.text: The biomagnification factor is the concentration in water over the concentration in the top predator.
options.misconception: defines biomagnification using water rather than prey

options.misconception: inverts the predator to prey ratio

options.text: Each step's factor is predator concentration over prey concentration, and the factors multiply as you move up the chain.

questions.topic: Half-life arithmetic on a fixed dump
questions.learningObjective: Apply half-life arithmetic to a concentration series.
questions.stem: Our revision sheet covers a fixed dump site where the contaminant level is measured once a year.

options.text: Subtract the same amount each year, since first-order loss removes a constant mass from a fixed pile.
options.misconception: assumes constant mass loss rather than exponential decay

options.text: Double the value each year, because the dump is receiving fresh deliveries from the operator each year.
options.misconception: assumes continuing input without stating it

options.text: Halve the value every half-life, so a level of 250 with a 120 day half-life falls to about 31 after a year.
Divide the value by the number of years, since a linear average describes long-term loss from a dump.
options.misconception: applies a linear average to exponential decay

questions.explanation: First-order decay halves the concentration after each half-life, so 250 becomes about 31 mg per kg over 360 days, three half-lives. Constant subtraction and linear averages misdescribe exponential loss.
questions.hint: Halve it once per half-life.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Chronic daily intake and hazard quotient
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a measured concentration becomes a chronic daily intake.
questions.stem: Set out, as a revision summary, how our group should work from a measured fish concentration to a chronic daily intake.

answer.exemplar: We would take the measured concentration in the edible fish tissue, multiply by the daily amount eaten by an average adult and by the number of days per year it is eaten, then divide by body weight and by the averaging time, which for a lifetime average equals the same exposure period. That gives a chronic daily intake to compare with the intake limit.

questions.explanation: A strong answer sets out concentration, intake rate, frequency and duration, then shows body weight and averaging time converting it to a per kilogram daily figure. A concentration alone never reaches an intake.
questions.hint: Concentration to intake needs four steps.

options.text: Add the absorbed doses from both pathways and compare the sum with the intake limit, rather than averaging the two.
Take the larger of the two pathways, because only the dominant route needs to be checked against the limit.
options.misconception: ignores the combined dose from both pathways

options.text: Average the two pathways, since a resident's body averages everything taken in by mouth and by drinking.
options.misconception: averages pathways instead of summing them

options.text: Assess each pathway separately against its own limit, because limits apply to single substances rather than doses.
options.misconception: treats pathways as independent of each other

questions.explanation: Exposure through different routes adds up in the body, so doses from both pathways should be summed before comparing with the intake limit. Averaging understates the total and dropping a pathway ignores exposure.
questions.hint: Doses from different routes accumulate.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the time needed for ninety percent depuration from fish tissue.
questions.stem: Our notes record a depuration half-life of 30 days in fish tissue, and we want to know how long until 90 percent has gone.
questions.explanation: Removing 90 percent leaves one tenth, and the time for that is 2.303 divided by the elimination constant 0.0231 per day, which gives about 99.7 days, or 3.3 half-lives.

options.text: The instrument response is drifting low, so the affected results need a check against reference material before use.
The samples are fine, because drift in a check standard cannot affect the sample readings.
options.misconception: believes drift affects only the standard

options.text: The batch should be rerun without adjustment, because drift means the calibration curve was never valid.
options.misconception: assumes an invalid curve from a drifting check

questions.explanation: A check standard reading below nominal is the classic sign of instrument drift, and samples analysed in that window carry a systematic bias. Verify the response against reference material first.
questions.hint: Check standards exist to catch drift.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a falling concentration in a growing fish.

stimulus.body: A fish sampled in March weighed 600 g and held 1.2 mg per kg of the contaminant. The same fish sampled in September weighed 900 g and held 0.9 mg per kg. The group notes that the fish was in clean water between the two dates, and that its diet changed with the seasons.

questions.stem: Using the series, how should our group interpret the fall in concentration between the two samples?

options.text: The concentration fell because the fish excreted the contaminant, since clean water removes body burden directly.
options.misconception: assumes clean water alone clears body burden

options.text: The concentration fell because the fish was older and therefore less able to store lipophilic contaminants.
options.misconception: claims age reduces storage of lipophilic compounds

options.text: The fall is a measurement error, because a fish in clean water should show no change in concentration.
options.misconception: assumes no change is expected in clean water

options.text: Growth dilution can explain much of the fall, because a larger fish with an unchanged burden shows a lower concentration.

questions.explanation: The fish gained mass between samples, and a fixed burden spread over more tissue gives a lower concentration, so growth dilution must be considered before claiming elimination. Diet change also affects uptake.
questions.hint: Check for growth before blaming elimination.

options.text: The limit is the no-effect level divided by a composite uncertainty factor of 1000, which is the usual arrangement.
The limit is the no-effect level divided by 100, and the extra factor of ten comes from a separate correction.
options.misconception: invents an unexplained extra factor

options.text: The limit is the no-effect level multiplied by a safety factor of 1000, which gives a more cautious result.
options.misconception: multiplies rather than divides by the factor

options.text: The two figures are unrelated, since no-effect levels and intake limits come from entirely separate sources.
options.misconception: denies the derivation link

questions.explanation: Dividing 0.4 by 1000 gives 0.0004 mg per kg per day, so the limit is the no-effect level reduced by a composite uncertainty factor covering species, individual, duration and database gaps.
questions.hint: Check which way the factor was applied.

options.text: Compare each route separately with the limit, since a limit applies to one route at a time.

Use whichever route gives the larger dose, since that is the one the body experiences.

options.misconception: merges two different ratios into one

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Half-life arithmetic on a fixed dump
questions.learningObjective: Infer a field half-life from a multi-decade soil series.

stimulus.body: A 1998 survey of the old landfill found the contaminant at 250 mg per kg in soil. A 2024 survey of the same plot reads 31.25 mg per kg. Laboratory work on the same soil gives a first-order half-life of 120 days for the compound. The record notes that no waste has been placed on the site since 1998.

questions.stem: Using the record, what does the fall in soil concentration tell the group?

options.text: The fall matches the laboratory half-life, so the laboratory figure can be used for future predictions.
options.misconception: concludes field and lab decay agree

options.text: The site cannot be closed, because the concentration is still above the level at which it started.
options.misconception: confuses a remaining level with an increasing one

options.text: The fall shows the compound is still breaking down quickly, so only a short closure period is needed.
options.misconception: misreads a slow decline as fast decay

options.text: A fall from 250 to 31.25 is three half-lives in 26 years, so observed decay is far slower than the laboratory rate.

questions.explanation: Three half-lives of 120 days cover about a year, so 26 years showing three halvings implies a field half-life far longer than the lab one. Field rates must be measured before closure periods are set.
questions.hint: Count the halvings the site record actually shows.

options.misconception: inverts body weight and intake rate

options.text: Concentration times intake rate, divided by the number of days in the exposure period only.
options.misconception: omits body weight and averaging time

options.text: Concentration divided by body weight, because body weight already accounts for how often food is eaten.
options.misconception: assumes body weight covers frequency and duration

options.text: Concentration times intake rate times frequency times duration, divided by body weight and by the averaging time.

questions.explanation: The chronic daily intake multiplies concentration by intake rate, frequency and duration, then divides by body weight and averaging time, converting a lifetime average into a daily figure. Missing steps change the answer.
questions.hint: Six terms, three of them divided out.

options.text: Keep the fish in contaminated water and sample them, since only continued exposure reveals the elimination rate.
options.misconception: confuses exposure with elimination in the design

options.text: Measure the water concentration only, since the tissue burden must follow the water by a fixed ratio.
options.misconception: assumes tissue tracks water with a fixed ratio

questions.explanation: The hazard quotient compares the estimated intake with the limit, so 0.0003 over 0.001 gives 0.3, and below one means the intake is under the planning level. Some exposure is expected and acceptable.
questions.hint: Divide the intake by the limit and read the quotient.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Combine background and site exposure within one allowance.
questions.stem: Our group is checking how the site exposure should be combined with a background contribution.

options.text: Compare the site contribution with the limit on its own, because background intake is outside the planning boundary.
options.misconception: excludes background intake from the budget

options.text: Add the background and site contributions, then compare the total with the limit, since the allowance is one budget.
Use the larger of the two, since only the dominant source determines whether the limit is exceeded.
options.misconception: ignores the smaller source's contribution

options.text: Subtract the background from the limit before comparing, which gives a tighter test of the site itself.
options.misconception: treats the limit as a site-specific allowance

questions.explanation: The intake limit is one allowance for the population, so background and site exposures must be added before the comparison. Comparing the site alone or subtracting the background misstate how much room is left.
questions.hint: The allowance covers every source together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the time for ninety-five percent depuration in fish tissue.
questions.stem: Our worksheet has fish clearing a contaminant with a depuration half-life of 20 days, and we need the time for 95 percent of the burden to go.
questions.explanation: Removing 95 percent leaves one twentieth, which takes 4.32 half-lives, since each halving divides by two, and 4.32 times 20 days gives 86.4 days. Ninety percent needs only 3.3 half-lives.
questions.hint: Work in halvings from what is left.

questions.learningObjective: Set the frequency of drift checks during a long analytical run.
questions.stem: Our group's laboratory manager asks how often analytical drift should be checked during a long sampling run.

options.text: Check the response repeatedly against reference material so that drift is seen as it develops, not after the run.
Once at the start is enough, because drift is always a warm-up effect that settles once the run begins.
options.misconception: assumes drift is only a warm-up effect

options.text: Only when a sample looks odd, because checking the instrument interrupts the run and wastes reagents.
options.misconception: prioritises cost over data quality

options.text: After the run, by comparing all results against the previous campaign, since drift cannot be seen in real time.
options.misconception: believes drift cannot be detected during a run

questions.explanation: Drift develops during a run, so checking the response against reference material at intervals reveals it while it happens and identifies which samples are affected. Checking only at the start leaves that window unknown.
questions.hint: Look for drift while it is still happening.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Write a method for interpreting age-related trends in fish tissue data.
questions.stem: Write a revision note explaining how our group should interpret a falling concentration in older fish from the same lake.

answer.exemplar: We would consider growth dilution first, since a fish that gains mass while its burden changes little shows a lower concentration per kilogram even though uptake continues. We would normalise the results for size and age, check that the diet change has not altered intake, and only then consider depuration as an explanation for the trend.

questions.explanation: A strong answer puts growth dilution first, then size and age normalisation, then the effect of diet change, and only after that treats depuration as an explanation. Attributing the fall straight to elimination ignores tissue growth.
questions.hint: Growth first, elimination only if it survives.
